problem: Mapless, target-driven visual navigation of wheeled mobile robots in dynamic, unknown environments lacks a clear comparison of DRL algorithms (value-based DQN vs policy-gradient A3C) using RGB and depth inputs.
motivation: Classical navigation depends on maps and hand-engineered pipelines, while DRL can map visual input directly to control commands. The paper compares DQN and A3C, including the effect of parallel threads, to see which suits WMR visual navigation in simulation before real-time transfer.
key_idea: Train and compare DQN and multi-threaded A3C agents, with RGB and depth inputs and a pre-trained ResNet50 feature extractor, for mapless target-driven TurtleBot2 navigation in ROS/Gazebo simulation.
insight: According to the abstract, A3C outperformed DQN, and A3C performance improved as threads increased from 4 to 6 to 8, so parallel actor-learners help. Only the abstract was available, so no ablation details or numbers can be cited.
method: DQN: value-learning deep Q-network producing control commands from RGB and depth images
A3C: asynchronous advantage actor-critic policy-gradient agent, run with 4, 6 and 8 computation threads
Simulation: OpenAI Gym Gazebo environments within ROS, with a Kobuki TurtleBot2
Feature extractor: pre-trained ResNet50, further trained on regrouped objects common in laboratory settings, for target-driven mapless navigation
Evaluation: reward statistics and completion time compared across three simulation environments

setting.backbone: DQN and A3C networks; pre-trained ResNet50 (further trained) for target-driven navigation
setting.training_data: Trained progressively in OpenAI Gym Gazebo simulation environments; ResNet50 further trained on regrouped lab-setting object images (scale not given in the abstract)
setting.action_space: discrete control commands for the TurtleBot2 (details not given in the abstract)

numbers_note: abstract only; no numeric results are given
results: In three simulation environments, A3C with 4, 6 and 8 threads outperformed DQN on reward statistics and completion time, and A3C improved with more threads. No numbers are given in the abstract.
limitations: Simulation only; real-time deployment through transfer learning is left as future work
Only two DRL algorithms and one robot platform are compared, with no standard navigation benchmark
